facts: Algeria is the largest country in Africa, a title it took from Sudan when South Sudan separated in 2011.
About four fifths of its territory is Sahara, so nearly the whole population lives on the northern coastal strip.
The Tassili n'Ajjer plateau holds thousands of prehistoric rock paintings showing a once-green Sahara.
Cabinda, Angola's oil-rich province, is an exclave separated from the rest of the country by DR Congo.
Angola is one of Africa's largest oil producers and a significant diamond exporter.
Portuguese is the official language, and Angola has one of the largest Portuguese-speaking populations in Africa.
Porto-Novo is the official capital, but Cotonou is the seat of government and the largest city.
The Kingdom of Dahomey, centred here, was known for its all-female military regiment.
Vodun originated in this region and remains an officially recognised religion in Benin.
The Kalahari covers around 70% of Botswana, a semi-arid sand basin rather than a true desert, and it supports grazing for much of the year.
The Okavango Delta is a rare inland delta, emptying into the desert instead of the sea.
Botswana went from one of the world's poorest countries at independence in 1966 to middle-income status, largely through diamonds.
The country's name, adopted in 1984, translates roughly as 'land of upright people'.
It is landlocked and largely flat savanna, with the Sahel across its northern reaches.
FESPACO in Ouagadougou is the largest African film festival on the continent.
Burundi moved its political capital from Bujumbura to Gitega in 2019.
It is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa and among the least urbanised.
Lake Tanganyika on its western border is the second deepest lake in the world.
Cabo Verde is an archipelago of ten volcanic islands about 570 kilometres off the West African coast.
The islands were uninhabited before Portuguese settlement in the 15th century.
More Cabo Verdeans live abroad than in the country itself, and remittances are a major part of the economy.
Cameroon is often called 'Africa in miniature' for containing desert, savanna, rainforest and mountains.
It has both English and French as official languages, a legacy of divided colonial rule.
Mount Cameroon is an active volcano and one of the wettest places on Earth.
The Central African Republic sits almost exactly at the centre of the African landmass.
It is rich in diamonds, gold and uranium yet remains among the world's least developed economies.
Sangha Trinational park, shared with Cameroon and Congo, protects largely undisturbed rainforest.
Lake Chad has shrunk by roughly 90% since the 1960s through drought and irrigation.
Emi Koussi is a dormant volcano in the Tibesti range, the highest point in the Sahara.
Chad is landlocked, and its capital lies over 1,000 kilometres from the nearest port.
The Comoros is a volcanic archipelago between Mozambique and Madagascar.
Mount Karthala has one of the largest active volcanic craters in the world.
It is one of the world's main producers of ylang-ylang, used in perfume.
Brazzaville and Kinshasa face each other across the Congo River, the closest pair of capital cities in the world.
About 60% of the country is rainforest, part of the Congo Basin.
Oil accounts for the large majority of export earnings, most of it pumped offshore near Pointe-Noire.
DR Congo is the second largest country in Africa and holds most of the Congo Basin rainforest.
It produces the majority of the world's cobalt, essential to rechargeable batteries.
The Congo River is the deepest river in the world, exceeding 220 metres in places.
Lake Assal is the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth.
Djibouti's position at the Bab-el-Mandeb strait makes it a strategic shipping chokepoint.
It hosts foreign military bases from several countries, more than almost any comparable state.
Around 95% of Egyptians live on roughly 5% of the land, along the Nile and its delta.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, carries a substantial share of global seaborne trade.
The Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one of the seven ancient wonders still standing.
Equatorial Guinea is the only sovereign African state where Spanish is an official language.
Its capital, Malabo, sits on the island of Bioko rather than the mainland.
Oil discoveries in the 1990s transformed it into one of Africa's largest per-capita oil producers.
Asmara's early-20th-century modernist architecture earned the city World Heritage status.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993 after a thirty-year war.
Its independence left Ethiopia landlocked, redrawing the region's trade routes.
Eswatini is one of the last absolute monarchies in the world.
It changed its name from Swaziland in 2018 to avoid confusion with Switzerland.
The country has two capitals: Mbabane is administrative and Lobamba is legislative and royal.
Ethiopia was never colonised, apart from a brief Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941.
It uses its own calendar with thirteen months and runs roughly seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one.
Coffee originates here, and the Ethiopian highlands remain a centre of arabica cultivation.
Around 88% of Gabon is forest, and 11% of its territory is protected national park.
Oil wealth gives it one of the higher per-capita incomes in sub-Saharan Africa.
The Oklo uranium deposit hosted a natural nuclear fission reaction around two billion years ago.
The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa, a narrow strip along its river.
It is surrounded by Senegal on three sides, with the Atlantic on the fourth.
Its borders roughly follow the navigable stretch of the Gambia River.
Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule, in 1957.
Lake Volta is among the largest reservoirs in the world by surface area.
It is a leading cocoa producer and was known as the Gold Coast for its mineral wealth.
Guinea holds the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the ore from which aluminium is made.
The Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers all rise in the Guinea Highlands.
It was the only French colony to reject de Gaulle's 1958 community proposal and take immediate independence.
Guinea-Bissau includes the Bijagós archipelago of around 88 islands, most of them uninhabited.
Cashew nuts dominate its exports and much of its rural economy.
Portuguese is official, but Guinea-Bissau Creole is the common everyday language.
Ivory Coast is the world's largest cocoa producer, supplying roughly 40% of global output.
The capital moved to Yamoussoukro in 1983, though Abidjan remains the economic centre.
The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is among the largest church buildings in the world.
The Great Rift Valley runs the length of Kenya and is dotted with soda lakes drawing millions of flamingos.
Kenya pioneered mobile money with M-Pesa, which reshaped banking across East Africa.
Its highland athletes have dominated middle- and long-distance running for decades.
Lesotho is one of only three countries entirely surrounded by a single other country.
It is the only country in the world with all its land above 1,000 metres.
It exports water to South Africa through the Lesotho Highlands Water Project.
Liberia was founded in the 1820s as a settlement for freed African Americans and declared independence in 1847.
Its capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe.
It operates one of the world's largest ship registries, so a large share of global tonnage flies its flag.
Libya is over 90% desert and has the largest proven oil reserves in Africa.
The Great Man-Made River pumps fossil groundwater from beneath the Sahara to the coastal cities.
Leptis Magna is among the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere in the world.
Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world and separated from other landmasses around 88 million years ago.
Roughly 90% of its wildlife exists nowhere else, including all of the world's lemur species.
Malagasy belongs to the Austronesian family, most closely related to languages of Borneo rather than Africa.
Lake Malawi covers about a fifth of the country and holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth.
Malawi is landlocked and one of the most densely populated countries in southern Africa.
It is often called the Warm Heart of Africa, a nickname tied to its tourism image.
Timbuktu was a centre of Islamic scholarship, with manuscript libraries dating from the 13th century onward.
The medieval Mali Empire controlled much of the trans-Saharan gold trade.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world and is replastered each year by the town.
Around three quarters of Mauritania is desert, and the Sahara continues to expand southward.
The Richat Structure, a huge circular formation in the desert, is a landmark for astronauts in orbit.
Its coastal waters are among the richest fishing grounds in West Africa.

highest.name: Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire

facts: The dodo was endemic to Mauritius and was driven extinct within a century of European arrival.
The island was uninhabited before Dutch settlement in the 17th century.
It has one of Africa's highest per-capita incomes, built on tourism, textiles and financial services.
Morocco has both Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines, separated by the Strait of Gibraltar.
The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, is often cited as the oldest continuously operating university.
The Atlas Mountains shield the fertile north from the Sahara to the south.
Mozambique has one of Africa's longest coastlines, stretching about 2,500 kilometres on the Indian Ocean.
Its flag is the only national flag to feature a modern rifle.
It joined the Commonwealth in 1995 without ever having been a British colony.
The Namib is considered the oldest desert in the world, arid for at least 55 million years.
Namibia was the first country to write environmental protection into its constitution.
The Caprivi Strip, a narrow eastward finger, was drawn to give German colonists access to the Zambezi.
More than 80% of Niger is Sahara, and it is one of the hottest countries on Earth.
It has among the highest birth rates in the world, giving it a very young population.
The Air and Ténéré reserve is one of the largest protected areas in Africa.
Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, with more people than any European nation.
Nollywood produces more films per year than almost any other film industry in the world.
The capital moved from Lagos to the purpose-built city of Abuja in 1991.
Rwanda is known as the land of a thousand hills for its steep, terraced landscape.
It banned single-use plastic bags in 2008, well ahead of most of the world.
Volcanoes National Park protects a substantial share of the remaining mountain gorillas.
São Tomé and Príncipe is the second smallest African country and sits almost on the equator.
The islands were uninhabited before Portuguese arrival in the 1470s.
Once the world's largest cocoa producer, it still relies heavily on the crop.
Senegal almost completely surrounds The Gambia, which follows its river inland.
Dakar sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of mainland Africa.
Gorée Island off Dakar is a memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.
Seychelles is the smallest African country by both population and land area.
Its inner islands are granite rather than coral or volcanic, a rarity for mid-ocean islands.
The coco de mer palm, found only here, produces the largest seed of any plant.
Freetown was founded in 1787 as a settlement for freed slaves from Britain, Nova Scotia and Jamaica.
Its natural harbour is among the largest in the world.
Sierra Leone's diamond fields funded the civil war of the 1990s, giving rise to the term blood diamonds.
Somalia has the longest mainland coastline in Africa, at around 3,300 kilometres.
It is one of the most linguistically and ethnically homogeneous countries on the continent.
Somaliland in the north has functioned self-governed since 1991 without international recognition.
South Africa has three capital cities: Pretoria for the executive, Cape Town for parliament and Bloemfontein for the judiciary.
It recognises twelve official languages, among the most of any country.
It completely surrounds Lesotho and produces a large share of the world's platinum.
South Sudan became independent in 2011 and is the world's youngest widely recognised country.
The Sudd, a vast wetland on the White Nile, is one of the largest in the world.
It is landlocked and depends on pipelines through Sudan to export its oil.
Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, built by the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë.
The Blue and White Niles meet at Khartoum to form the main Nile.
It was Africa's largest country until South Sudan separated in 2011.
Kilimanjaro is the highest point in Africa and the tallest free-standing mountain in the world.
Tanzania borders three of Africa's great lakes: Victoria, Tanganyika and Malawi.
The country was formed in 1964 by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar.
Togo is one of Africa's narrowest countries, roughly 115 kilometres wide but 550 long.
It is among the world's largest producers of phosphate rock.
Koutammakou, in the north, is known for its fortified mud tower-houses.
Tunisia is the northernmost country in Africa and the smallest in the Maghreb.
Carthage, near modern Tunis, was Rome's great rival before its destruction in 146 BC.
Parts of the Sahara here have stood in for other planets in numerous films.
Uganda shares Lake Victoria, the largest lake in Africa, with Kenya and Tanzania.
The Nile's most commonly cited source is at Jinja, where it leaves Lake Victoria.
The Rwenzori range, the Mountains of the Moon, carries glaciers despite sitting on the equator.
Zambia borders eight countries, more than any other in southern Africa.
Victoria Falls on the Zambezi forms the largest sheet of falling water in the world.
Copper has dominated its economy since the colonial era, and the Copperbelt remains its industrial heart.
Great Zimbabwe, a stone city built between the 11th and 15th centuries, gave the country its name.
Hyperinflation in 2008 forced the abandonment of the Zimbabwean dollar for nearly a decade.
Lake Kariba on the Zambezi is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world by volume.
